name: How long does multifamily construction take in Los Angeles from design to occupancy?

mainEntity.name: What is the realistic timeline for a multifamily project in Los Angeles County, from first drawings through permits and final certificate of occupancy?
mainEntity.text: What is the realistic timeline for a multifamily project in Los Angeles County, from first drawings through permits and final certificate of occupancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: The total timeline for multifamily construction in Los Angeles County usually includes predesign, schematic design, entitlement or zoning review, permit plan check, bidding or GMP negotiation, construction, inspections, and final closeout. The construction phase itself may look straightforward, but the project often starts months or even more than a year before crews mobilize. The biggest schedule risks are permit revisions, utility company coordination, structural redesign, and long-lead materials. If the project is in a dense city like Glendale, Pasadena, Burbank, or North Hollywood, access, staging, and inspection scheduling can also slow progress. Mixed-use or subterranean parking projects generally require more time than simple low-rise apartment buildings. Owners should request a schedule that separates design, permitting, and field work instead of a single completion date. A credible builder will explain what can be compressed and what cannot. Good scheduling also includes time for tenant relocation, demolition, weather delays, and final sign-offs. If a proposal promises a highly compressed timeline without discussing permits, utility review, or inspection sequencing, it is likely incomplete.
acceptedAnswer.description: A multifamily project in Los Angeles County often takes much longer than owners expect because design, entitlement, plan check, utility coordination, and inspections can each add months. The construction phase may be only part of the schedule; preconstruction and permitting frequently determine the real finish date. Small projects can move faster, but complex sites, add-ons, or mixed-use elements usually extend the timeline.
